summary: For children aged 8–9, this procedural Earth-science topic teaches pupils to organise seasonal weather data (daily temperature, precipitation, cloud cover and wind direction over a month) into a table, build a pictograph or bar graph from it, and read the display to describe what weather is TYPICAL of a season — comparing seasons as evidence. The emphasis is on experiencing the full raw-readings → table → graph → interpretation procedure, on 'typical/most-common' as distinct from any single day, and on keeping displays to pictographs and bar graphs. Climate change and long-term trends are explicitly out of scope at this level.
misconceptions: Treating one unusual day as representative of the whole season instead of the typical pattern.
Miscounting pictograph icons (ignoring that one symbol may stand for several days).
Confusing the tallest bar with the answer to every question, regardless of what is asked.
Thinking 'typical' means the single highest or lowest value rather than the most common.
Mixing weather (short-term) with climate/long-term trends, which are out of scope here.

activities.title: Weather-data studio: sort, table, graph, describe
steps: Start with a month of daily weather cards, each showing a temperature, a rain-or-dry mark, cloud cover and a wind arrow, presented mixed together.
Sort the cards and organise the readings into a data table (temperature, precipitation/cloud cover, wind).

Build a bar graph or pictograph from the table — for a pictograph, first fix what one icon stands for (e.g. one icon = one day, or several days per icon) and then apply that key consistently to every icon when counting totals; for a bar graph, use a uniform equal-interval scale and label the axes.

Read the finished graph to state the typical/most-common condition for the season (e.g. 'most winter days were between 3 and 7°C', or 'this summer had more dry days than this winter' if the graphs show that).
Place two seasons' graphs, drawn with the same scale and the same temperature bands, side by side and compare them, saying how the shapes differ and which season is which.
Point to the specific part of your graph that shows one season is warmer than the other, using the display itself as the evidence.
Decide whether one unusually cold day changes which season the data represents, and explain why the typical pattern across the whole month still identifies the season.
Consider how confident the description would be with only a few days of data versus a full month, and explain why more readings make the typical pattern clearer.
Discuss how the display would look different if rainfall rather than temperature had been measured (e.g. counts of rainy versus dry days), to see that the chosen variable shapes the chart.
Check that the display, not memory of 'summer is hot', is used as the evidence for every statement.
activities.insight: The shape of an organised graph answers a question the scattered raw cards cannot: the tallest bar or bars, showing the temperature band or bands with the most days, make it obvious what is typical of a season, and placing two graphs drawn on the same scale side by side makes seasonal comparison much easier. 'Typical' means the most-common pattern across the whole month, not a single unusual day, and more days of data make that pattern clearer.

activities.title: Read and compare seasonal weather graphs
steps: Read a given seasonal bar graph or pictograph and answer what temperature or condition was most typical.
Match each season to its bar graph from a set.
Order a set of seasonal graphs by rainfall, from least to most.
Answer varied questions about the same graph (not only 'which bar is tallest?') so the question asked determines which bar to read.
activities.insight: Fluently reading pictographs and bar graphs — identifying the most-common condition, matching displays to seasons, and comparing across seasons — is a core part of the standard's goal of using displays to describe typical seasonal weather.

activities.title: Annotated graph walkthrough: the parts of a chart
steps: Explore an annotated bar graph or pictograph, revealing what the axes, bars/icons and key each mean.
Name what one icon stands for in the pictograph's key and how to use it to count a total.
Identify where the scale intervals and labels are, before building a graph of your own.
activities.insight: A bar chart/pictograph has named parts — axes, scaled intervals, bars or icons, and a key — and understanding each part is a step towards building and reading displays accurately.

checkQuestion: Here is a month of daily weather cards (temperature and rain) for two different seasons, mixed together. Sort them, put each season's data into a table, make a bar chart of the temperatures, then tell me which season is which and how your chart shows it.
checkAnswer: The child sorts the cards by season, organises them into a table, produces a correctly-scaled and labelled bar chart, and reads it to describe the typical conditions — e.g. 'this season is warmer, most bars are higher; the other has more rainy days' — using the display as the evidence.
